# Class 7: not everyone shares a slope

> **A note on the data.** Same file as Class 6: the repeated body-size measurements on the
> Lundy sparrows. Class 6 used tarsus length as the predictor and freed the intercept. Today
> we free the slope, and the first thing the class does is discover, in a cell, that tarsus is
> the wrong column to try it on. The one failure on the page happened when it was built, and is shown as it happened.

---

## Objectives

By the end of this class you should be able to:

1. Say what a random slope frees, and check *before you fit it* whether your covariate varies enough **within** groups for the question to have an answer.
2. Fit `(1 + x | group)` and read the two standard deviations and the correlation out of the covariance block the engine returns.
3. Explain why the intercept–slope correlation changes, and can change sign, when you move the origin of the covariate without changing the model.
4. Compare a random-slope model against a random-intercept model with AIC and with a likelihood-ratio test, and say why the usual reference distribution is wrong when the thing you are testing is a variance.
5. Describe what shrinkage does to a group's *slope*, and say why a group with three measurements keeps only a little of the slope its own points suggest.
6. Split a repeated-measures covariate into its within-group and between-group parts, and say what a single coefficient on the unsplit covariate is a blend of.

---

## The class

**Itchy's office, 9:00 am. TOTO has come straight from Class 6 with the caterpillar plot still open on the laptop. MOMO is here early with a question she wrote down last week and did not ask. EDDIE has brought a dunnock dataset he intends to break. JARO is in the corridor and will be needed by the end of the hour.**

**Itchy:** Last week I drew you a picture and said one sentence about it that I want back before we start. Toto. The picture with all the bird lines in it.

**Toto:** They were all parallel.

**Itchy:** All parallel. Every bird got to sit high or low; none of them got its own steepness. That was the restriction, and you could see it in the plot. Today we take it out. But not the way you are about to.

**Momo:** Meaning we do not just type it.

**Itchy:** Meaning we do not just type it. A random slope asks whether the relationship between *y* and *x* differs from group to group. Before you can ask that, *x* has to differ within a group; otherwise there is nothing for a per-bird slope to be estimated *from*, and the software will find that out about ninety seconds after you do, in a worse mood. So: file first.

### Which column actually moves within a bird

```{julia}
#| label: setup
#| output: false
include("../tools/figures.jl")
using DRM, DataFrames, CSV, Statistics, Random, LinearAlgebra, Printf, CairoMakie
using Distributions: Chisq, ccdf
set_theme!(theme_itchy(:light))

raw = CSV.read("../data/2012/BodySize.csv", DataFrame; missingstring = "NA")

# Class 6's cleaning, one column different: today's covariate is mass, so the
# rows we need complete are wing and weight.
sparrows = dropmissing(raw, [:Wing, :Weight])
w_bar = mean(sparrows.Weight)
sparrows.wc = sparrows.Weight .- w_bar     # mass, centred on its own mean

# Each bird's own mean mass, and each capture's departure from it. The last
# section of this class needs both; nothing before it does.
bird_mass = combine(groupby(sparrows, :BirdID), :Weight => mean => :m)
joined = leftjoin(sparrows, bird_mass, on = :BirdID)
sparrows.wbar = joined.m .- w_bar          # the bird's own average mass, centred
sparrows.wdev = sparrows.Weight .- joined.m   # this capture, relative to that bird

mkpath("../data/ch7")
CSV.write("../data/ch7/sparrows-weight.csv", sparrows)

n = nrow(sparrows)
bird_ids = sort(unique(sparrows.BirdID))
birds = length(bird_ids)
row_of = Dict(b => i for (i, b) in enumerate(bird_ids))
gi = [row_of[b] for b in sparrows.BirdID]      # each row's bird, as an index
nothing
```

**Itchy:** The file, cleaned as Class 6 cleaned it, except that the column we need complete today is mass rather than tarsus. Two new things in the cell. `leftjoin(sparrows, bird_mass, on = :BirdID)` attaches each bird's mean mass to every one of its rows, matching on the identifier: a **join** does what Class 6's `Dict` did by hand. And the cell ends with `nothing`, which is how you stop a cell printing its last value when that value is a whole data frame.

```{julia}
#| label: counts
@printf("rows %d on %d birds\n\n", n, birds)

per_bird = combine(groupby(sparrows, :BirdID), nrow => :k)
for k in sort(unique(per_bird.k))
    @printf("%3d birds measured %d times\n", count(==(k), per_bird.k), k)
end
k_med = median(per_bird.k)
@printf("\nmedian measurements per bird: %.1f\n", k_med)
```

**Momo:** Two, three or four. That is not a lot of points to fit a line through.

**Itchy:** It is not, and hold that thought until the caterpillar, where it becomes the whole lesson. First: which of these columns moves *within* a bird? You already have the tool. A repeatability is the share of variance that sits **between** individuals, so one minus it is the share that sits within. The cell loops over five columns and stores what it finds in two lookup tables: `Dict{Symbol,Float64}()` is an empty `Dict` that will hold a number under each column's name, filled by `share_within[c] = ...`. `Float64.(...)` converts a column to plain decimals. And inside `combine`, `:y => (v -> ...) => :sw` is Class 1's double arrow with an anonymous function in the middle, here one that returns `missing` for a bird measured only once, which `skipmissing` then steps over.

```{julia}
#| label: within-bird
candidates = [:Tarsus, :BillL, :BillW, :Tail, :Weight]
share_within = Dict{Symbol,Float64}()
within_sd = Dict{Symbol,Float64}()

@printf("%-8s %6s %8s %8s %12s\n", "column", "rows", "R", "1 - R", "within SD")
for c in candidates
    d0 = dropmissing(sparrows, [c])
    d = DataFrame(BirdID = d0.BirdID, y = Float64.(d0[!, c]))
    R = repeatability(drm(bf(@formula(y ~ 1 + (1|BirdID))), Gaussian(); data = d)).estimate
    share_within[c] = 1 - R
    g = combine(groupby(d, :BirdID),
                :y => (v -> length(v) > 1 ? std(v) : missing) => :sw)
    within_sd[c] = mean(skipmissing(g.sw))
    @printf("%-8s %6d %8.4f %8.4f %12.4f\n",
            c, nrow(d), R, 1 - R, within_sd[c])
end
```

**Toto:** Tarsus is nearly all between.

**Itchy:** Tarsus is `{julia} string(round(100 * share_within[:Tarsus], digits = 1), "%")` within a bird and the rest between, which is Class 6's number arriving as a warning. A grown sparrow's leg bone does not change between captures, so a per-bird slope *on tarsus* asks `{julia} birds` birds for the steepness of a line through points stacked on top of each other. Mass is near the other end of the table: `{julia} string(round(100 * share_within[:Weight], digits = 1), "%")` of the variation in mass is a bird differing from itself.

**Eddie:** Because mass is condition and tarsus is architecture.

**Itchy:** Because mass is condition and tarsus is architecture, and that distinction is worth more than today's arithmetic.

**Momo:** Then why mass? Bill width has a larger within-bird share than mass does. It is the largest in the table.

**Itchy:** It is, and I am glad you read the whole column rather than the row I pointed at, because that is the trap in this table. **A share does not tell you what the variation is made of.** A grown sparrow's bill width is architecture too; its within-bird share is large because the trait is a couple of millimetres wide and the calipers are not that precise, so most of what moves between captures is the measuring, not the bird. Look at the two numbers together: bill width moves `{julia} string(round(Int, 100 * share_within[:BillW]), "%")` of its variation within a bird, and that movement is `{julia} round(within_sd[:BillW], digits = 4)` of a millimetre. Mass genuinely changes: a sparrow is heavier after a good week and lighter after a bad one, and `{julia} round(within_sd[:Weight], digits = 3)` grams of within-bird movement is a bird, not a ruler.

**Momo:** So the rule is not "pick the biggest share".

**Itchy:** The rule is: **pick a covariate whose within-group variation is a thing that happens, not a thing you did.** Then check that its share is large enough to estimate from. Mass passes both. So today's covariate is **mass**, and today's question is: when a bird is heavier, is its wing measured longer, and **by the same amount in every bird**? Look at it before you model it.

::: {#fig-spaghetti-data}

```{julia}
k_of = Dict(r.BirdID => r.k for r in eachrow(per_bird))
repeat_ids = [b for b in bird_ids if k_of[b] >= 3]

# Every twelfth bird in the ordering by mean mass: a rule, not a preference.
mean_mass = [mean(sparrows.Weight[sparrows.BirdID .== b]) for b in repeat_ids]
shown = repeat_ids[sortperm(mean_mass)][1:12:length(repeat_ids)]

fig = Figure(size = (520, 380))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "mass (g)", ylabel = "wing (mm)",
    title = "$(length(shown)) birds, each caught at least three times")
scatter!(ax, sparrows.Weight, sparrows.Wing; markersize = 4, color = (:grey, 0.3))
# One colour per bird; line style and marker shape are second and third channels.
# Style cycles on 3, marker on 4 (coprime with style's 3) so the two
# non-colour channels alone never repeat together within any run of 12
# birds — two birds sharing a style still land on different markers.
palette = to_value(Makie.current_default_theme().palette.color)
styles  = [:solid, :dash, :dashdot]
markers = [:circle, :rect, :utriangle, :diamond]

for (i, b) in enumerate(shown)
    rows = sortperm(sparrows.Weight[sparrows.BirdID .== b])
    m = findall(sparrows.BirdID .== b)[rows]
    col = palette[mod1(i, length(palette))]
    ls = styles[mod1(i, length(styles))]
    mk = markers[mod1(i, length(markers))]
    scatter!(ax, sparrows.Weight[m], sparrows.Wing[m]; markersize = 10, color = col, marker = mk)
    lines!(ax, sparrows.Weight[m], sparrows.Wing[m]; color = (col, 0.7), linewidth = 1.4, linestyle = ls)
end
fig
```

Every twelfth bird, in the ordering by mean mass, among those measured at least three times, with each bird's own captures joined in order of mass. A bird's identity is its colour, line style and marker shape together, so that no two of the `{julia} length(shown)` birds shown share all three. Grey is the whole file. A random slope is the claim that these little segments do not all have the same steepness.

:::

**Toto:** Some of them go up and some of them go down.

**Itchy:** Some of them go up and some of them go down, and *that* is the picture of the thing we are about to put a number on. Whether the up-and-down is real or is what three points do when you join them is the content of the hour.

### The slope you have been sharing

**Itchy:** Two fits, in order of how much they let the birds get away with. Watch the slope, and watch its standard error, because Class 6 left you a promise about it that I have to keep today.

```{julia}
#| label: two-fits-wc
pooled_fit = drm(bf(@formula(Wing ~ wc)),                   Gaussian(); data = sparrows)
ri_fit     = drm(bf(@formula(Wing ~ wc + (1|BirdID))),      Gaussian(); data = sparrows)

@printf("%-16s %10s %10s %12s\n", "", "slope", "SE", "residual SD")
for (nm, f) in (("no bird at all", pooled_fit), ("+ (1|BirdID)", ri_fit))
    @printf("%-16s %10.4f %10.4f %12.4f\n",
            nm, coef(f, :mu)[2], stderror(f)[2], first(sigma(f)))
end
b_pooled, se_pooled = coef(pooled_fit, :mu)[2], stderror(pooled_fit)[2]
b_ri, se_ri = coef(ri_fit, :mu)[2], stderror(ri_fit)[2]
s_pooled = first(sigma(pooled_fit));
```

**Momo:** The standard error went **down**. Last week it went up.

**Itchy:** Last week it went up, and last week I told you it would not always. Read the third column.

**Toto:** The residual standard deviation collapsed.

**Itchy:** From `{julia} round(s_pooled, digits = 4)` millimetres to `{julia} round(first(sigma(ri_fit)), digits = 4)`, which is a factor of `{julia} round((s_pooled / first(sigma(ri_fit)))^2, digits = 1)` in residual *variance*. **Two things happen at once when you add `(1 | g)`**: you stop counting repeated measurements as fresh evidence, which pushes the standard error up, and you take an enormous amount of noise out of the residual, which pulls it down. Class 6 showed you the first one winning, on a predictor that barely moves within a bird. Which one wins is not settled by which side of one half the within-share falls on — mass is `{julia} string(round(100 * (1 - share_within[:Weight]), digits = 1), "%")` between-bird, and the second still wins: the standard error falls to `{julia} round(se_ri / se_pooled, digits = 3)` of what it was, a cut of `{julia} string(round(100 * (1 - se_ri / se_pooled), digits = 1), "%")`. Keep the two mechanisms; do not keep an arithmetic test.

**Toto:** And the slope halved.

**Itchy:** The slope more than halved, from `{julia} round(b_pooled, digits = 4)` to `{julia} round(b_ri, digits = 4)` millimetres of wing per gram, which is a bigger move than anything Class 6 showed you. That is the second thing this predictor is doing, and it is bigger than today's subject. The pooled line is answering a blend of two questions — heavier birds are bigger birds, and a given bird gains and loses mass — and putting a bird term in the model changes the blend without separating it. **We will separate it, on this page, in the last section of the class.** Everything between here and there is fitted on the blended model, and the last section shows you which numbers move when we pull it apart.

### Freeing the slope

> **μ_ij = (β0 + u_0j) + (β1 + u_1j) x_ij, with (u_0j, u_1j) ~ N(0, Σ) and y_ij ~ N(μ_ij, σ²)**
>
> **Σ = [σ_0², ρ σ_0 σ_1 ; ρ σ_0 σ_1, σ_1²]**

**Itchy:** Measurement *i* on bird *j*, and the same six symbols as Class 6 with two additions. u_0j is the bird's own nudge to the intercept, which is exactly last week's u_j. u_1j is the bird's own nudge to the **slope**, and it is new. They are drawn together, from a two-dimensional normal, so there are three numbers in Σ rather than one: σ_0 the spread of intercepts, σ_1 the spread of slopes, and ρ the correlation between a bird's intercept and its slope.

**Eddie:** Three numbers, and the model gained two parameters rather than one.

**Itchy:** Two: σ_1 and ρ. Remember that, because it is what the test is testing. In code it is one term, and you have seen the shape of it before.

```{julia}
#| label: fit-uncentred
#| error: true
drm(bf(@formula(Wing ~ Weight + (1 + Weight|BirdID))), Gaussian(); data = sparrows)
```

**Toto:** That is not a warning, that is a crash.

**Itchy:** That is a crash, and I put it in front of you because you will meet it on your own data this week. It is this engine's optimiser failing on a covariate whose zero sits far outside its range — an arithmetic failure inside the software, not a fact about the model, and the next section proves that with a number; the post-mortem is in [Where the engine stops](appendix-b-engine.html). The fix is to centre. Same model, `Weight` replaced by `wc` in both places it appears, and nothing else.

```{julia}
#| label: fit-centred
rs_fit = drm(bf(@formula(Wing ~ wc + (1 + wc|BirdID))), Gaussian(); data = sparrows)
rs_fit
```

**Toto:** `wc` instead of `Weight`. That is the centred one from the setup cell.

**Itchy:** Mass minus its own mean, `{julia} round(w_bar, digits = 3)` grams, and nothing else. Same data, same response, same formula shape, same family. One fit dies and one converges, and the only difference is where zero is.

**Momo:** That cannot be a real difference between models.

**Itchy:** It is not a real difference between models, and I am going to prove that in the next ten minutes with a number. Read the new block first. There is no `resd` line this time; there is a random-effect covariance block, printed in the form the optimiser works with rather than as σ_0, σ_1 and ρ. `vc(fit)` hands you Σ itself, and the next cell takes the three numbers out of it: `V[1, 1]` is row one, column one of a matrix, `V[1, 2]` the entry beside it.

```{julia}
#| label: read-the-block
V = vc(rs_fit)[:BirdID]                      # the 2x2 covariance of (intercept, slope)
sd0, sd1 = sqrt(V[1, 1]), sqrt(V[2, 2])
rho = V[1, 2] / (sd0 * sd1)
sigma_e = first(sigma(rs_fit))
b_rs = coef(rs_fit, :mu)

@printf("sigma_0 (spread of bird intercepts) : %.4f mm\n", sd0)
@printf("sigma_1 (spread of bird slopes)     : %.4f mm per g\n", sd1)
@printf("rho     (their correlation)         : %+.4f\n", rho)
@printf("sigma   (within a bird)             : %.4f mm\n\n", sigma_e)
@printf("population slope beta1              : %.4f   SE %.4f\n",
        b_rs[2], stderror(rs_fit)[2])
```

**Toto:** So a bird's own slope is the population slope plus its nudge, and the nudges have a standard deviation of `{julia} round(sd1, digits = 4)`.

**Itchy:** Which you should immediately compare with the population slope itself, `{julia} round(b_rs[2], digits = 4)`. The spread of the slopes is larger than the average slope: taken at face value, a good number of these birds have a *negative* slope while the average bird has a positive one. Whether to take it at face value is the second half of the hour.

### The correlation you did not ask for

**Momo:** I want to go back. You said you could prove the crash was not a real difference between models.

**Itchy:** And ρ is how. Fit the same model at four origins, changing nothing else — twenty grams, twenty-four, the mean, thirty. `at_origin` does one fit and ends with `return` and a NamedTuple, the explicit way of saying what a function hands back; `map(at_origin, origins)` calls it on each origin and collects the four results, which is a comprehension by another name.

```{julia}
#| label: origins
function at_origin(origin)
    d = DataFrame(BirdID = sparrows.BirdID, Wing = sparrows.Wing,
                  x = sparrows.Weight .- origin)
    f = drm(bf(@formula(Wing ~ x + (1 + x|BirdID))), Gaussian(); data = d)
    W = vc(f)[:BirdID]
    s0, s1 = sqrt(W[1, 1]), sqrt(W[2, 2])
    return (; sd0 = s0, sd1 = s1, rho = W[1, 2] / (s0 * s1),
            sigma = first(sigma(f)), aic = aic(f), b1 = coef(f, :mu)[2])
end

origins = [20.0, 24.0, w_bar, 30.0]
@printf("%-14s %9s %9s %9s %9s %12s\n",
        "x = mass -", "sigma_0", "sigma_1", "rho", "sigma", "AIC")
rows = map(at_origin, origins)
for (o, r) in zip(origins, rows)
    @printf("%-14.3f %9.4f %9.4f %+9.4f %9.5f %12.4f\n",
            o, r.sd0, r.sd1, r.rho, r.sigma, r.aic)
end
@printf("\nlargest AIC difference across the four : %.3e\n",
        maximum(r.aic for r in rows) - minimum(r.aic for r in rows))
@printf("largest slope difference across the four: %.3e\n",
        maximum(r.b1 for r in rows) - minimum(r.b1 for r in rows))
```

**Toto:** The correlation changed sign.

**Itchy:** The correlation changed sign, from `{julia} round(rows[1].rho, digits = 4)` at twenty grams to `{julia} round(rows[end].rho, digits = 4)` at thirty. And read the last two columns before anyone gets excited: σ_1 is the same to four decimal places in every row, σ is the same, the slope is the same, and the AIC differs by `{julia} @sprintf("%.0e", maximum(r.aic for r in rows) - minimum(r.aic for r in rows))`. **These are not four models. This is one model, written down four ways.**

**Momo:** Then what is ρ a statement about?

**Itchy:** ρ is the correlation between a bird's slope and its intercept, and its **intercept is its predicted wing length at x equal to zero**. Move zero and you are asking about the bird's wing length at a different mass, so of course the correlation changes. At twenty grams, which is below every bird in the file, "intercept" means an extrapolation backwards, and a bird with a steeper slope necessarily extrapolates to a lower value — hence a negative correlation, manufactured by the arithmetic. At thirty grams the tilt goes the other way for the same reason. At the mean, ρ is closest to being about the birds and not about the origin. So: report ρ with its origin in the same sentence, and centre a covariate whose zero is outside its range, every time.

**Toto:** Show me the sign change instead of making me read it off a column.

**Itchy:** Fair — ρ is a function of one number, where you put zero, and a function of one number is a curve, not four separate fits. Shifting the origin by `a` is a change of coordinates with a known formula, so the curve comes from the one Σ we already have, without refitting anything.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-origin-rho
#| fig-cap: "The correlation ρ as a continuous function of where mass is centred, computed from the one fitted Σ by a change of coordinates, with no refitting. It crosses zero where the curve meets the dotted line: negative to the left, positive to the right. The four diamonds are the four origins from the table above, each labelled with its ρ. The shaded strip is the mass this file actually contains; twenty grams sits outside it, which is why ρ there is an extrapolation backwards."
# Moving the origin by a: u0' = u0 + a*u1, so Var(u0') = s0^2 - 2a*Cov + a^2*s1^2
# and Cov' = Cov - a*s1^2. sigma_1 and the likelihood cannot move.
shifted(a) = [V[1,1] - 2a*V[1,2] + a^2*V[2,2]   V[1,2] - a*V[2,2]
              V[1,2] - a*V[2,2]                 V[2,2]]
rho_at(t) = (S = shifted(-t); S[1, 2] / sqrt(S[1, 1] * S[2, 2]))
t_zero = -V[1, 2] / V[2, 2]                      # where the correlation is exactly zero
t_grid = range(minimum(origins) - w_bar - 1, maximum(origins) - w_bar + 1, length = 200)
origin_t = origins .- w_bar

fig = Figure(size = (520, 380))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "origin, as mass minus $(round(w_bar, digits = 1)) g (g)",
    ylabel = "correlation ρ", title = "One curve, not four fits")
vspan!(ax, minimum(sparrows.wc), maximum(sparrows.wc); color = (:grey, 0.08))
hlines!(ax, [0.0]; linestyle = :dot, color = (:grey, 0.6))
lines!(ax, t_grid, rho_at.(t_grid); linewidth = 2)
scatter!(ax, origin_t, [r.rho for r in rows]; markersize = 11, marker = :diamond)
for (t, r) in zip(origin_t, rows)
    text!(ax, t, r.rho; text = string(round(r.rho, digits = 2)),
        align = (:center, :bottom), offset = (0, 8), fontsize = 12)
end
fig
```

**Itchy:** `{julia} round(t_zero + w_bar, digits = 2)` grams — that is where ρ is exactly zero, not at some special boundary, just the one mass at which the curve crosses its own axis. Left of it, negative; right of it, positive; and the four points are the four rows of that table, now impossible to mistake for four different models.

**Momo:** Then what is the ρ we have?

**Itchy:** `{julia} round(rho, digits = 4)`, at a mass of `{julia} round(w_bar, digits = 3)` grams, and the honest reading is: birds that are longer-winged at average mass tend, mildly, to gain more measured wing per gram. Mildly. Look at its standard error in the R box later on before you write a sentence about it.

### Is the extra term worth it

**Itchy:** Two models, nested, one estimator. Toto, before we test anything, the cheap comparison.

```{julia}
#| label: compare-aic
npar(f) = round(Int, (aic(f) + 2 * loglik(f)) / 2)     # AIC = 2k - 2 logLik

@printf("%-22s %8s %12s %12s\n", "", "params", "logLik", "AIC")
for (nm, f) in (("wc + (1|BirdID)", ri_fit), ("wc + (1 + wc|BirdID)", rs_fit))
    @printf("%-22s %8d %12.4f %12.4f\n", nm, npar(f), loglik(f), aic(f))
end
d_aic = aic(ri_fit) - aic(rs_fit)
@printf("\nAIC drops by %.4f for two extra parameters\n", d_aic)
```

**Toto:** That is a big drop.

**Itchy:** It is a big drop, and AIC has already charged us two parameters for it. Now the test. I am going to ask the naive question first and read what the engine says back.

```{julia}
#| label: naive-lrt
lrtest(ri_fit, rs_fit)
```

**Momo:** It gave me the number and told me not to use it.

**Itchy:** σ_1 cannot be negative, so testing it at zero is a test on the boundary of the parameter space, and χ² with two degrees of freedom is not the right reference. Class 8 takes the boundary apart properly; today you need the one fact that fits this step, and Jaro is in the corridor.

**Jaro:** *(from the doorway)* You want the mixture. Self and Liang (1987) worked out what the likelihood-ratio statistic does when the null value sits on the boundary of the parameter space; Stram and Lee (1994) applied it to the mixed model, and their result is stated for exactly the step you have just taken — a model with *q* random effects against the same model with *q* plus one. Here *q* is one. Of the two parameters you added, the variance sits on a boundary and the correlation does not — and when the variance goes to zero the correlation stops existing at all. For that case the null is a **fifty-fifty mixture of chi-squared with one degree of freedom and chi-squared with two**. One line of arithmetic.

```{julia}
#| label: boundary-lrt
stat = 2 * (loglik(rs_fit) - loglik(ri_fit))

# Stram & Lee (1994): q random effects against q + 1. For q = 1 the null is a
# 50:50 mixture of chi-squared with 1 and 2 degrees of freedom.
p_sl(s) = 0.5 * ccdf(Chisq(1), s) + 0.5 * ccdf(Chisq(2), s)

@printf("LR statistic                                  : %.4f\n\n", stat)
@printf("naive chi-squared(2)                          : %.3e\n", ccdf(Chisq(2), stat))
@printf("Stram & Lee mixture, 0.5 chi2(1) + 0.5 chi2(2): %.3e\n", p_sl(stat))
```

**Toto:** Both tiny.

**Itchy:** Both tiny, and notice that *first*, because it means nothing in this paragraph changes the decision. When the numbers are not tiny, the ordering matters: the naive reference is the conservative one — it loses power rather than inventing significance — and the mixture is the right one for this step. The engine's own boundary correction is built for independent variances, a different mixture and not this case; [Where the engine stops](appendix-b-engine.html) says which is which. **Read the assumptions on a correction before you take its p-value.**

**Momo:** And if I still do not believe σ_1? How do I know the model would not find a spread of slopes in data that has none?

**Itchy:** You simulate a world with none, refit the bigger model, and count how often it says otherwise — a parametric bootstrap of the test, which Class 8 builds.

### What the model does to a bird's own slope

**Eddie:** Here is what I want to know. The model says the spread of slopes is `{julia} round(sd1, digits = 3)`. If I fit a line through one bird's own points, do I get its slope?

**Itchy:** You do not, and the gap is the lesson. Take the birds with at least three captures, fit each bird's own line by least squares with nothing borrowed from anybody, and put those next to what the model predicts for the same birds.

```{julia}
#| label: own-slopes
B = ranef(rs_fit)[:BirdID]                 # birds x 2: column 1 intercepts, column 2 slopes
model_slope = b_rs[2] .+ B[:, 2]

own_slope = Dict{String,Float64}()
for b in repeat_ids
    m = sparrows.BirdID .== b
    x, y = sparrows.wc[m], sparrows.Wing[m]
    own_slope[b] = cov(x, y) / var(x)
end

ols = [own_slope[b] for b in repeat_ids]
mod = [model_slope[row_of[b]] for b in repeat_ids]

@printf("birds with at least three captures : %d of %d\n\n", length(repeat_ids), birds)
@printf("%-24s %9s %9s %9s\n", "", "SD", "min", "max")
@printf("%-24s %9.4f %9.4f %9.4f\n", "each bird on its own",   std(ols), minimum(ols), maximum(ols))
@printf("%-24s %9.4f %9.4f %9.4f\n", "the model's slopes",     std(mod), minimum(mod), maximum(mod))
@printf("%-24s %9.4f %9.4f %9.4f\n", "the model, all birds",
        std(model_slope), minimum(model_slope), maximum(model_slope))
@printf("%-24s %9.4f\n", "sigma_1 from the fit", sd1)
@printf("\nSD ratio, model to own: %.4f\n", std(mod) / std(ols))

# Two birds worth reading together, both found from the data rather than
# named by hand: the tightest mass spread of any bird with three or more
# captures, and the bird whose own slope is the most extreme.
xspread = Dict(b => std(sparrows.Weight[sparrows.BirdID .== b]) for b in repeat_ids)
tightest = argmin(xspread)
worst = repeat_ids[argmin(ols)]
@printf("tightest spread  %s: masses %s, within-bird SD %.4f (file average %.4f), own slope %.4f\n",
        tightest, string(sparrows.Weight[sparrows.BirdID .== tightest]),
        xspread[tightest], within_sd[:Weight], own_slope[tightest])
@printf("worst own slope  %s: masses %s, within-bird SD %.4f, own slope %.4f\n",
        worst, string(sparrows.Weight[sparrows.BirdID .== worst]),
        xspread[worst], own_slope[worst])
```

**Toto:** The birds' own slopes are enormous. One of them is nearly minus six.

**Itchy:** One of them is nearly `{julia} round(minimum(ols), digits = 2)` millimetres of wing per gram, which would mean a sparrow's wing shortening by half a centimetre when it eats. It is not real, and the two printed lines name the pair that shows why. `{julia} tightest` has the tightest mass spread of any bird with three or more captures — `{julia} round(xspread[tightest], digits = 4)` grams, against the file's average of `{julia} round(within_sd[:Weight], digits = 4)` — and its own slope came out at `{julia} round(own_slope[tightest], digits = 4)`. `{julia} worst` has an almost identical spread, `{julia} round(xspread[worst], digits = 4)` grams, and its own slope is `{julia} round(own_slope[worst], digits = 4)`. Two birds with near-identical, tiny mass spreads, one dead flat and one falling off a cliff: that is what dividing a difference in wing by a difference in mass that small buys you. Draw it.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-slope-shrinkage
#| fig-cap: "Class 6's caterpillar, now for slopes. Circles are each bird's own least-squares slope from its points alone; diamonds are what the model predicts for the same bird. The legend keeps Class 6's wording: read 'raw mean' as the bird's own unshrunk estimate and 'BLUP' as the model's shrunk one. Every sixth bird in the ordering by its own slope is shown, a rule and not a preference."
sel = sortperm(ols)[1:6:length(repeat_ids)]

fig = fig_shrinkage(repeat_ids[sel], ols[sel], mod[sel])
fig.content[1].ylabel = "slope of wing on mass (mm per g)"
fig.content[1].title = "Shrinkage, now for slopes"
fig
```

**Eddie:** The diamonds are almost flat.

**Itchy:** The diamonds are almost flat, the circles are all over the plot, and the ratio of their spreads is `{julia} round(std(mod) / std(ols), digits = 3)`. A bird keeps roughly a quarter of the slope its own points suggest. That is not the model being timid; it is the model observing that three points and a within-bird spread of about one gram cannot tell it much, and weighting accordingly — Class 6's arithmetic, applied to a slope instead of a mean.

**Momo:** Then why is the spread of the model's slopes over all `{julia} birds` birds, `{julia} round(std(model_slope), digits = 4)`, smaller than σ_1, which is `{julia} round(sd1, digits = 4)`?

**Itchy:** Because a predicted effect is shrunk and a variance component is not. σ_1 is the model's estimate of how much bird slopes *really* differ; the spread of the predictions is how much the model is willing to *say* they differ given the evidence in front of it. The second is the smaller of the two **in expectation**, in every mixed model you will ever fit. Quoting the spread of the predicted slopes as if it were σ_1 is a common enough mistake that people have written papers about it. And compare like with like: `{julia} round(std(mod), digits = 4)` is over the `{julia} length(repeat_ids)` birds with three captures or more, `{julia} round(std(model_slope), digits = 4)` is over all `{julia} birds`. Now the same fit drawn as lines, which is the picture that names the chapter.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-bird-lines
#| fig-cap: "One population line, and one line per bird. Compare with Class 6's version of this figure, where every line was parallel."
xs = range(minimum(sparrows.wc), maximum(sparrows.wc), length = 50)

fig = Figure(size = (520, 380))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "mass, centred (g)", ylabel = "wing (mm)",
    title = "$(birds) intercepts and $(birds) slopes")
scatter!(ax, sparrows.wc, sparrows.Wing; markersize = 4, color = (:grey, 0.3))
for j in 1:birds
    lines!(ax, xs, (b_rs[1] + B[j, 1]) .+ (b_rs[2] + B[j, 2]) .* xs;
        color = (:grey, 0.20), linewidth = 0.6)
end
lines!(ax, xs, b_rs[1] .+ b_rs[2] .* xs; linewidth = 3)
fig
```

**Toto:** They fan out.

**Itchy:** They fan out, and they cross, which parallel lines cannot do. That is the constant this class freed, visible.

### Is the model any good

**Itchy:** Residuals, and there is a trap here that is the same trap as Class 6 wearing a different hat. Ask for the residual the book has taught you to plot in every family.

```{julia}
#| label: quantile-residuals
rq = residuals(rs_fit; type = :quantile, rng = MersenneTwister(70))

@printf("SD of the quantile residuals : %.4f   (it should be 1)\n", std(rq))

# The model's own marginal SD, row by row, with every bird effect set to zero:
# Var(y) = sigma_0^2 + 2 rho sigma_0 sigma_1 x + sigma_1^2 x^2 + sigma^2.
marg = V[1, 1] .+ 2 .* V[1, 2] .* sparrows.wc .+ V[2, 2] .* sparrows.wc .^ 2 .+ sigma_e^2
@printf("sqrt(mean(marginal var))/sigma: %.4f\n", sqrt(mean(marg)) / sigma_e)
```

**Momo:** It is twice what it should be. Is the model that bad?

**Itchy:** The model is not bad; the residual is not the one you think. `fitted` on these fits is **marginal** — the population line, with every bird effect set to zero — exactly as it was in Class 6. So a quantile residual here compares each wing to a distribution that has had the birds removed from its mean but not from its spread, and it divides by σ, which is the *within*-bird spread. Of course it comes out about `{julia} round(sqrt(mean(marg)) / sigma_e, digits = 1)` times too wide: that is the ratio the model itself predicts, printed in the second line. Nothing is wrong with the model. You are holding the wrong residual.

**Eddie:** So subtract the bird's own predicted line, like last week.

**Itchy:** Subtract the bird's own predicted line — both parts of it now, the intercept nudge and the slope nudge — and you have the conditional residual, which is what σ is a claim about. And before you draw anything, look for the rows that are a long way from their own bird, because two are in this file and they will set the scale of the plot if you let them.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-worm
#| fig-cap: "Worm plot of the conditional residuals, standardised by their own spread with the two flagged rows left out of the divisor and left in the plot. The vertical axis is deviation from the normal quantile, so a well-behaved model gives a flat line inside the band. The two points at the bottom left are the two rows named in the printout above."
cond = sparrows.Wing .- fitted(rs_fit) .- B[gi, 1] .- B[gi, 2] .* sparrows.wc

@printf("SD of conditional residuals : %.4f   (sigma is %.4f)\n", std(cond), sigma_e)
@printf("shortfall                   : %.1f%%\n\n", 100 * (1 - std(cond) / sigma_e))

# Rows more than three residual SDs from their own bird's line, named.
bad = findall(abs.(cond ./ std(cond)) .> 3)
keep = setdiff(1:n, bad)
for i in bad
    b = sparrows.BirdID[i]
    m = sparrows.BirdID .== b
    @printf("%s recorded at Wing %.1f; its own wings %s at masses %s\n",
            b, sparrows.Wing[i], string(sparrows.Wing[m]), string(sparrows.Weight[m]))
end

# Standardise by a spread those rows cannot set, then count what sits outside
# the same pointwise band the figure draws.
sd_clean = std(cond[keep])
z = cond ./ sd_clean
zz = sort(z); pp = ((1:n) .- 0.5) ./ n
theo = sqrt(2) .* erfinv_approx.(2 .* pp .- 1)
band = 2 .* sqrt.(pp .* (1 .- pp) ./ n) ./ (exp.(-theo .^ 2 ./ 2) ./ sqrt(2pi))
outside = count(abs.(zz .- theo) .> band)
lowest_two = sparrows.BirdID[sortperm(z)[1:2]]
@printf("\npoints outside the pointwise band : %d of %d\n", outside, n)
@printf("the two lowest residuals belong to : %s\n", join(lowest_two, ", "))

fig_diagnostic(z; title = "within-bird residuals, random-slope fit")
```

**Toto:** Short of σ again.

**Itchy:** Short of σ again, and for Class 6's reason, which now applies twice over: a shrunk prediction removes slightly *less* than the bird's real effect, so some of it stays behind in the residual, and here two per-bird numbers are being subtracted, neither at full strength. So the plot is good for one thing and not the other: it can tell you whether the within-bird wobble is symmetric and normal-ish and free of trend, and it cannot tell you whether σ is right.

**Momo:** Then read it, because those two points at the bottom left are a long way out.

**Itchy:** They are the two rows the cell named — `{julia} outside` points sit outside the band, and the two lowest residuals belong to `{julia} join(lowest_two, " and ")` — and the rest of the worm stays inside the band. One is a bird recorded at sixty-seven millimetres whose other three wings are all in the middle seventies; the other is four to six millimetres below its own three. Wing in this file is a whole number in `{julia} string(round(Int, 100 * mean(sparrows.Wing .== round.(sparrows.Wing))), "%")` of rows, so σ of `{julia} round(sigma_e, digits = 4)` millimetres is close to the recording granularity, and a dropped digit is a live hypothesis alongside a broken primary or a bird caught mid-moult. **This is a finding about the file, not about random slopes**, so I am naming it, leaving it in the plot, and sending it to Exercise 7. Two things you may not do: quote σ from this fit as if those rows belonged in it, and read a worm plot standardised by a spread that the outliers you are looking for helped to set.

### One box, and it is earned

**Itchy:** An R-trained reader will type this model in `lmer` and get a printed correlation with a standard error next to it, which our engine does not give you. That is worth one box, because the correlation is the parameter this chapter has spent twenty minutes warning you about.

> **↔ TRANSLATE: the same fit in R, and one thing R prints that Julia does not**
>
> `drmTMB` is the R twin of this engine and takes the identical formula inside the identical
> `bf()` box. It reaches the same maximum — the same two standard deviations, correlation, σ
> and log-likelihood — and *adds* a printed **correlation with a standard error**, which
> DRM.jl does not report. That is an absence in the Julia engine, not a disagreement.
>
> `lme4::lmer` is here for comparison only. Its default is REML and ours is ML, so its
> variance components come out slightly larger; pass `REML = FALSE` and it lands on our
> numbers. Class 8 spends its hour on that difference.
>
> The block below was run once by hand, on the date shown, against the file this chapter's
> first cell writes; it does not re-run when the page is built. The script is kept at
> `data/ch7/ch7-r-box.R`.

R 4.6.0 | drmTMB 0.7.0 | lme4 2.0.1 | 459 rows, 171 birds

drmTMB (estimator: ML)
  sd(intercept) 1.7177  (SE 0.1201)
  sd(slope)     0.4308  (SE 0.0768)
  correlation   +0.2354  (SE 0.1383)   <- printed, with a standard error

lme4::lmer, same formula
  default (REML)     sd0 1.7233  sd1 0.4353  cor +0.2335  sigma 1.0180  logLik -875.5085

**Momo:** The correlation's standard error is bigger than half the correlation.

**Itchy:** The standard error is more than half the estimate, which is the sentence I wanted you to reach on your own. ρ depends on where zero is, it changes sign, and on top of that, on `{julia} birds` birds with a median of `{julia} round(Int, k_med)` captures each, it sits under two standard errors from zero. **Fit the correlation because leaving it out constrains the model; do not build a story on it.**

### The slope that was doing two jobs

**Itchy:** Last section, the one I promised you an hour ago. Momo, my own sentence, back at me.

**Momo:** That the pooled line was answering a blend of two questions, and that putting a bird term in the model changed the blend without separating it.

**Itchy:** And every number since has been fitted on the blend. So let us separate it, because it takes one line and one parameter. Split mass into two columns: the bird's **own average mass**, a fact about the bird, and each capture's **departure from that average**, a fact about the day. Then give them separate coefficients.

```{julia}
#| label: mundlak
# wbar and wdev were built in the setup cell: wbar is the bird's own mean mass
# (centred), wdev is this capture minus that mean. They are orthogonal by
# construction, and wbar + wdev = wc, so nothing has been added to the data.
sep_ri = drm(bf(@formula(Wing ~ wdev + wbar + (1|BirdID))),         Gaussian(); data = sparrows)
sep_rs = drm(bf(@formula(Wing ~ wdev + wbar + (1 + wdev|BirdID))), Gaussian(); data = sparrows)

W = vc(sep_rs)[:BirdID]
sd1_sep = sqrt(W[2, 2])
rho_sep = W[1, 2] / (sqrt(W[1, 1]) * sd1_sep)
bs, ses = coef(sep_ri, :mu), stderror(sep_ri)

@printf("%-30s %7s %10s %9s %9s %11s\n", "", "params", "logLik", "sigma_1", "rho", "AIC")
for (nm, f, s1, r) in (("wc + (1|BirdID)",           ri_fit, NaN, NaN),
                       ("wc + (1 + wc|BirdID)",      rs_fit, sd1, rho),
                       ("wdev + wbar + (1|BirdID)",  sep_ri, NaN, NaN),
                       ("wdev + wbar + (1 + wdev|.)", sep_rs, sd1_sep, rho_sep))
    @printf("%-30s %7d %10.4f %9s %9s %11.4f\n", nm, npar(f), loglik(f),
            isnan(s1) ? "-" : @sprintf("%.4f", s1),
            isnan(r)  ? "-" : @sprintf("%+.4f", r), aic(f))
end

@printf("\nwithin-bird slope  : %+.4f   SE %.4f   z %5.2f\n", bs[2], ses[2], bs[2] / ses[2])
@printf("between-bird slope : %+.4f   SE %.4f   z %5.2f\n", bs[3], ses[3], bs[3] / ses[3])
@printf("they differ by     : %+.4f\n\n", bs[3] - bs[2])

lr_sep = 2 * (loglik(sep_rs) - loglik(sep_ri))
@printf("AIC bought by ONE extra fixed parameter : %.4f\n", aic(ri_fit) - aic(sep_ri))
@printf("AIC bought by TWO random-slope parameters: %.4f\n", aic(ri_fit) - aic(rs_fit))
@printf("LR for the slope, blended  : %.4f  (p %.3e)\n", stat, p_sl(stat))
@printf("LR for the slope, separated: %.4f  (p %.3e)\n", lr_sep, p_sl(lr_sep))
@printf("share of the blended LR that was fixed-effect misspecification: %.1f%%\n",
        100 * (1 - lr_sep / stat))
```

**Toto:** The two slopes are nothing like each other.

**Itchy:** Nothing like each other. Between birds, `{julia} round(bs[3], digits = 4)` millimetres of wing per gram, with a *z* of `{julia} round(bs[3] / ses[3], digits = 1)`: bigger birds are heavier birds and have longer wings, which is not news and is not a question anyone needed a random slope to ask. Within a bird, `{julia} round(bs[2], digits = 4)`, with a standard error of `{julia} round(ses[2], digits = 4)` and a *z* of `{julia} round(bs[2] / ses[2], digits = 2)`. **On this file there is no detectable within-bird effect of mass on wing at all.** And the blended coefficient I have been reading to you all morning, `{julia} round(b_rs[2], digits = 4)`, sits between them, because that is what a blend does.

**Momo:** Then the sentence you said earlier, that longer-winged birds gain more measured wing per gram, was about the wrong thing.

**Itchy:** It was reading a between-bird fact as a within-bird one, the oldest mistake in the repeated-measures literature, and I let it stand for an hour so that you would see what a blend does when nobody splits it. Now read the third row of the table, which should annoy you most.

**Eddie:** One extra fixed parameter buys `{julia} round(aic(ri_fit) - aic(sep_ri), digits = 2)` of AIC. The whole random slope buys `{julia} round(aic(ri_fit) - aic(rs_fit), digits = 2)` for two.

**Itchy:** One parameter, more AIC, and it beats the model this chapter has been building all morning with one parameter fewer. **The cheapest thing on this page was never the random slope. It was noticing that a covariate with a within part and a between part is two covariates.** That is worth more to you than anything else I have said today, and it belongs in every repeated-measures model you fit.

**Momo:** And what happens to σ_1?

**Itchy:** This is the good part. Fit the random slope **on the separated model** — a per-bird slope on the *within* column, which is the only column a within-bird slope could sensibly be on.

**Toto:** σ_1 fell from `{julia} round(sd1, digits = 4)` to `{julia} round(sd1_sep, digits = 4)`, and ρ went from `{julia} round(rho, digits = 4)` up to `{julia} round(rho_sep, digits = 4)`.

**Itchy:** A cut of `{julia} string(round(Int, 100 * (1 - sd1_sep / sd1)), "%")` in the headline number of the hour, and the mechanism is one line of algebra: a per-bird slope on the blended column multiplies **both** parts, u_1j times the within deviation *and* u_1j times the bird's own mean. So in the blended model the slope variance had to absorb the between-versus-within contrast that the fixed part refused to separate. It was doing two jobs. Give the fixed part its second coefficient and σ_1 goes back to doing one.

**Eddie:** And the test?

**Itchy:** The likelihood-ratio statistic falls from `{julia} round(stat, digits = 2)` to `{julia} round(lr_sep, digits = 2)`, so **`{julia} string(round(Int, 100 * (1 - lr_sep / stat)), "%")` of the evidence I showed you for random slopes was evidence for a misspecified fixed part.** The subject survives — read the p-value: `{julia} @sprintf("%.1e", p_sl(lr_sep))` on the separated model, against the same fifty-fifty mixture, and AIC still prefers the random slope by `{julia} round(aic(sep_ri) - aic(sep_rs), digits = 2)`. **Birds really do differ in slope on this file**, by `{julia} string(round(Int, 100 * sd1_sep / sd1), "%")` of what the blended model said. What changed is not the finding. It is the size of it, and where it came from.

**Momo:** So what do I write in a paper?

**Itchy:** The separated model's numbers, because they come from the model that actually asks the within-bird question: AIC improves by `{julia} round(aic(sep_ri) - aic(sep_rs), digits = 2)` for the random slope, and the boundary-corrected p is `{julia} @sprintf("%.1e", p_sl(lr_sep))`. And the order to do it in, which is the sentence to take home: **fit the decomposition first, then ask whether the within slope varies.** That is Exercise 1.

**Itchy:** One note and then the summary. This engine does not yet fit a random slope for a binomial response; [Where the engine stops](appendix-b-engine.html) has the detail. When it does, everything on this page transfers, except that you will read the two standard deviations on the log-odds scale.

**Toto:** So today's summary is: not everyone shares a slope.

**Itchy:** Today's summary is: not everyone shares a slope, the model will tell you how much they differ, and it will charge you two parameters and one correlation you have to interpret carefully.

## Summary

### Stats stuff

- **What a random slope frees.** `(1 + x | g)` lets each group have its own steepness as well as its own height; the group lines stop being parallel and start crossing.
- **Check the covariate before you fit.** A random slope needs *x* to vary **within** groups; one minus the repeatability of *x* is the share that does, and what that variation *is* matters as much as its size: bill width moves within a bird because the calipers do, mass because the bird does.
- **Two parameters, not one.** A random slope adds a variance **and** a covariance, and the model comparison must charge for both.
- **Standard errors can go either way.** Adding `(1 | g)` stops counting repeated measurements as fresh evidence, which raises the standard error, and removes noise from the residual, which lowers it; here the residual variance fell by a factor of `{julia} round((s_pooled / first(sigma(ri_fit)))^2, digits = 1)` and the standard error fell with it.
- **The intercept–slope correlation is a statement about where zero is.** Move the origin of *x* and ρ changes, and can change sign, while the likelihood, the AIC, σ, σ_1 and the fixed slope do not move at all. Report ρ with the origin in the same sentence, or do not report it.
- **Centre a covariate whose zero is outside its range, every time.** With a far-away origin the fit can fail outright — an arithmetic failure in the optimiser, not a boundary — and centring removes it without changing the model.
- **Shrinkage, now for slopes.** A group's predicted slope is pulled hard towards the population slope when the group has few measurements or little spread in *x*; here groups keep about `{julia} string(round(Int, 100 * std(mod) / std(ols)), "%")` of the slope their own points suggest, and the spread of the predictions is not σ_1.
- **Testing σ_1 = 0 is a boundary problem, and the mixture matters.** The naive χ²(2) is conservative. Stram and Lee's (1994) result covers exactly this step, *q* random effects against *q* + 1, and gives a fifty-fifty mixture of χ²(1) and χ²(2); read the assumptions of any correction before you take its p-value.
- **Marginal residuals again.** `fitted` and `residuals` on these fits are population-level, so a quantile residual comes out about `{julia} round(sqrt(mean(marg)) / sigma_e, digits = 1)` times too wide; subtract *both* of the group's own numbers for the conditional residual, and read its worm plot for shape, not for σ, because shrinkage leaves part of each group effect behind.
- **Never read a worm plot through a standardiser the outliers helped to set.** Find the rows far from their own group first, name them, and divide by a spread they cannot move.
- **A coefficient on a repeated-measures covariate is a blend of two slopes, and splitting them costs one parameter.** Here the between-bird slope was `{julia} round(bs[3], digits = 3)` and the within-bird slope `{julia} round(bs[2], digits = 3)`, and the split bought more AIC for one parameter than the random slope bought for two.
- **A random slope on an unsplit covariate does two jobs.** Its variance absorbs the between-versus-within contrast the fixed part refused to separate; separating them cut σ_1 by `{julia} string(round(Int, 100 * (1 - sd1_sep / sd1)), "%")` and the random slope survived. **Fit the decomposition first; then ask whether the within slope varies.**
- **Maximal or parsimonious.** Barr et al. (2013) argue for the maximal random-effects structure; Bates et al. (2015) argue that over-parameterised structures should be reduced. This chapter is a small worked example: the maximal model wins by AIC, and most of the case for it evaporated when the fixed part was specified properly.

### Julia you used

- **`leftjoin(df, other, on = :BirdID)`.** Attaches the columns of `other` to every row of `df` whose key matches. The join that replaces a hand-built `Dict`.
- **`nothing` as a cell's last line.** Stops the cell printing a value nobody needs to see.
- **`Dict{Symbol,Float64}()` and `d[k] = v`.** An empty lookup table with declared key and value types, filled one entry at a time. `argmin(d)` on a Dict returns the *key* of the smallest value.
- **`:y => (v -> cond ? a : missing) => :sw`.** An anonymous function inside `combine`, and `missing` as a value a later `skipmissing` steps over. `Float64.(col)` converts a column element by element.
- **`V[1, 2]`.** Row one, column two of a matrix. `B[:, 2]` is the whole second column; `[a b; c d]` writes a small matrix by hand.
- **`return (; sd0 = s0, ...)` and `map(f, xs)`.** An explicit return of a NamedTuple, and a function applied to each element of a list with the results collected.
- **`[b for b in ids if k_of[b] >= 3]`.** A comprehension with a filter. `Dict(r.BirdID => r.k for r in eachrow(df))` builds a lookup from a frame walked row by row.
- **`findall(v)`, `setdiff(1:n, bad)`.** The positions where a true/false vector is true, and one set of positions with another removed.
- **`isnan(x) ? "-" : @sprintf("%.4f", x)`.** The one-line `if` again, with `@sprintf`, which is `@printf` returning a string instead of printing it.

### Calls you used

- `@formula(y ~ x + (1 + x|g))`: the random slope. Everything else about the call is unchanged from Class 6.
- `vc(fit)[:g]`: the 2 × 2 covariance of a correlated block; the diagonal's square roots are σ₀ and σ₁, the off-diagonal over their product is ρ. Why `re_sd` is empty here is in [Where the engine stops](appendix-b-engine.html).
- `ranef(fit)[:g]`: groups by terms — intercept deviations in column one, slope deviations in column two, in the order of `sort(unique(df.g))`.
- `aic(fit)`, `loglik(fit)`, `lrtest(reduced, full)`: the comparison and the naive test, which warns when the extra parameters include a variance. The Stram and Lee mixture is one line of `Distributions`: `0.5 * ccdf(Chisq(1), s) + 0.5 * ccdf(Chisq(2), s)`.
- `residuals(fit; type = :quantile, rng = MersenneTwister(seed))`: seeded, and marginal on a mixed fit.

## Further reading

*Graded by depth. Checked on 2026-09-07 against OpenAlex, an open catalogue of research papers.*

1. **Schielzeth, H. & Forstmeier, W. (2009) "Conclusions beyond support: overconfident estimates in mixed models", *Behavioral Ecology* 20:416–420.** doi:10.1093/beheco/arn145. Start here. The ecological case for today's chapter: leaving a random slope out of a model with repeated measures inflates confidence in the fixed effect. Short, concrete, and about animals.
2. **Barr, D. J., Levy, R., Scheepers, C. & Tily, H. J. (2013) "Random effects structure for confirmatory hypothesis testing: Keep it maximal", *Journal of Memory and Language* 68:255–278.** doi:10.1016/j.jml.2012.11.001. One half of the argument: fit the random-effects structure the design justifies, including the slopes, or your fixed-effect test is anticonservative. Read it with item 3 open beside it.
3. **Bates, D., Kliegl, R., Vasishth, S. & Baayen, H. (2015) "Parsimonious mixed models", arXiv:1506.04967.** doi:10.48550/arxiv.1506.04967. The other half, and **not** the lme4 paper Class 8 will cite, despite the year and the first author. It argues that maximal models are routinely over-parameterised; this chapter's example is the last section, where a random slope was carrying a fixed effect that had not been specified. A preprint, widely cited, never in a journal.
4. **Matuschek, H., Kliegl, R., Vasishth, S., Baayen, H. & Bates, D. (2017) "Balancing Type I error and power in linear mixed models", *Journal of Memory and Language* 94:305–315.** doi:10.1016/j.jml.2017.01.001. The referee between items 2 and 3, with simulations rather than assertions.
5. **Stram, D. O. & Lee, J. W. (1994) "Variance components testing in the longitudinal mixed effects model", *Biometrics* 50:1171–1177**, doi:10.2307/2533455, **with its published correction, *Biometrics* (1995) 51:1196**, doi:10.2307/2533038. The direct source for the mixture used in class, stated for exactly this step: *q* random effects against *q* + 1. Read the correction as well as the paper.
6. **Self, S. G. & Liang, K.-Y. (1987) "Asymptotic properties of maximum likelihood estimators and likelihood ratio tests under nonstandard conditions", *Journal of the American Statistical Association* 82:605–610.** The theory underneath item 5; open it once to see why the mixture has the weights it has.
7. **Gelman, A. & Hill, J. (2007) *Data Analysis Using Regression and Multilevel/Hierarchical Models*.** Chapters 12 and 13 for varying slopes drawn six ways, and for the between-versus-within decomposition at book length. Ignore the software.

## Exercises

```{julia}
#| label: exercise-checks
#| echo: false
#| output: false
# Numbers the exercise checks quote, computed from the named file.
ex_td = CSV.read("../data/ch8/tadpoles.csv", DataFrame)
ex_J = length(unique(ex_td.pond))
ex_pm = combine(groupby(ex_td, :pond), :days => mean => :m)
ex_joined = leftjoin(ex_td, ex_pm, on = :pond)
ex_td.dc = ex_td.days .- mean(ex_td.days)
ex_td.dmean = ex_joined.m .- mean(ex_td.days)
ex_td.ddev = ex_td.days .- ex_joined.m
ex_days_fit = drm(bf(@formula(days ~ 1 + (1|pond))), Gaussian(); data = ex_td)
ex_days_within = 1 - repeatability(ex_days_fit).estimate
ex_ri = drm(bf(@formula(length ~ dc + (1|pond))), Gaussian(); data = ex_td)
ex_sep = drm(bf(@formula(length ~ ddev + dmean + (1|pond))), Gaussian(); data = ex_td)
ex_rs = drm(bf(@formula(length ~ dc + (1 + dc|pond))), Gaussian(); data = ex_td)
ex_V = vc(ex_rs)[:pond]
ex_sd1 = sqrt(ex_V[2, 2])
ex_rho = ex_V[1, 2] / (sqrt(ex_V[1, 1]) * ex_sd1)
ex_stat = 2 * (loglik(ex_rs) - loglik(ex_ri))
ex_p_naive = lrtest(ex_ri, ex_rs).pvalue
ex_p_mix = p_sl(ex_stat)
ex_rho_at = Dict{Float64,Float64}()
for o in (0.0, 40.0)
    ex_td.dx = ex_td.days .- o
    f = drm(bf(@formula(length ~ dx + (1 + dx|pond))), Gaussian(); data = ex_td)
    W = vc(f)[:pond]
    ex_rho_at[o] = W[1, 2] / sqrt(W[1, 1] * W[2, 2])
end
ex_B = ranef(ex_rs)[:pond]
ex_groups = unique(ex_td.pond)
ex_model_slope = coef(ex_rs, :mu)[2] .+ ex_B[:, 2]
ex_own_slope = [(x = ex_td.dc[ex_td.pond .== g]; y = ex_td.length[ex_td.pond .== g];
                 cov(x, y) / var(x)) for g in ex_groups]
ex_spread_ratio = std(ex_model_slope) / std(ex_own_slope)
ex_gi = [findfirst(==(g), ex_groups) for g in ex_td.pond]
ex_cond = ex_td.length .- fitted(ex_rs) .- ex_B[ex_gi, 1] .- ex_B[ex_gi, 2] .* ex_td.dc
ex_flagged = count(abs.(ex_cond ./ std(ex_cond)) .> 3)
```

Graded by depth: the first three take ten minutes each. The exercises run on Momo's tadpole file, `data/ch8/tadpoles.csv`, which Class 8 simulates from a stated seed and says so: `{julia} nrow(ex_td)` tadpoles in `{julia} ex_J` ponds, each with its `days` since hatching and its body `length` — a grouped dataset with a covariate that varies within groups, so that nobody is stopped for want of one. Do every exercise on your own organism as well where you have one. A *check* is a number computed from that file when this page was built. **For every question, paste your code and then explain in your own words what each line does**, as if to somebody who has done Class 6 and not Class 7.

1. **Within and between, in the right order.** Centre `days` on its mean, then split it as the chapter split mass: each pond's own mean, and each tadpole's departure from it (`combine`, `leftjoin`, two subtractions). Fit `length ~ ddev + dmean + (1 | pond)` against `length ~ dc + (1 | pond)`. Report the two fixed slopes with their standard errors and the AIC of both fits. Two sentences: which of the two slopes the unsplit coefficient was closer to, and how much AIC the extra fixed parameter bought. *Check:* within-pond slope `{julia} round(coef(ex_sep, :mu)[2], digits = 3)`, between-pond slope `{julia} round(coef(ex_sep, :mu)[3], digits = 3)`, unsplit `{julia} round(coef(ex_ri, :mu)[2], digits = 3)`; the split changes AIC by `{julia} round(aic(ex_sep) - aic(ex_ri), digits = 2)`.

2. **Check before you fit.** Compute one minus the repeatability of `days` itself, the share of its variation that lives within ponds, as the chapter's table did for every candidate. Then say in one sentence whether `days` is a thing that happened to each tadpole or a thing that happened to each pond, and why that decides whether a random slope on it is a question with an answer. *Check:* the within share is `{julia} round(ex_days_within, digits = 2)`.

3. **Both fits, one term.** Fit `length ~ dc + (1 | pond)` and then `(1 + dc | pond)`. Before you look, predict whether the standard error on the slope will rise or fall. Report both fixed slopes, both standard errors, the residual SD of each fit, and the covariance block from `vc`; then explain whichever way the standard error went with **both** effects from class. *Check:* σ₁ = `{julia} round(ex_sd1, digits = 3)` and ρ = `{julia} round(ex_rho, digits = 2)`; the standard error moves from `{julia} round(stderror(ex_ri)[2], digits = 4)` to `{julia} round(stderror(ex_rs)[2], digits = 4)`.

4. **The right mixture.** Compare the two fits of question 3 with `lrtest`, then with the Stram and Lee mixture `p_sl` computed by hand as the chapter did. Report both p-values. Write two sentences saying which one you would report and why, **without** using the word "conservative" on its own — say what it is conservative *about*. Then say what the data-generating process in Class 8's cell tells you the right answer was. *Check:* naive p = `{julia} round(ex_p_naive, digits = 2)`, mixture p = `{julia} round(ex_p_mix, digits = 2)`.

5. **Move the origin.** Refit the random-slope model with `days` measured from zero, from its mean, and from day 40, which is beyond the data. Report σ₀, σ₁, ρ and the AIC for each, and say which of the four moved. *Check:* ρ runs from `{julia} round(ex_rho_at[0.0], digits = 2)` at day zero to `{julia} round(ex_rho_at[40.0], digits = 2)` at day 40, and σ₁ and the AIC do not move at all.

6. **The caterpillar, for slopes.** Compute each pond's own least-squares slope from its points alone, and plot them against the model's slopes as the chapter's figure did. Report the ratio of the two spreads. Which pond moved furthest, and is that because it had the fewest tadpoles, the least spread in `days`, or the most extreme own slope? The numbers decide; say which one you checked. *Check:* the model's slopes have `{julia} round(ex_spread_ratio, digits = 2)` of the spread of the ponds' own slopes.

7. **Two rows, or a shape?** Compute the conditional residuals of the random-slope fit and, before you draw anything, count the rows more than three residual SDs from their own pond's line. Draw the worm plot. Then two sentences: what you would do with any flagged rows, and why a file simulated from a Gaussian is the wrong place to expect any. *Check:* `{julia} ex_flagged` rows flagged.
